rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.4 and 3.1 <U+2013> authors build a GMS/MODFLOW groundwater model of Qalyubia Governorate, calibrate it in steady state against 11 observation wells for 2014 (Fig. 7) and verify with 5 wells (Fig. 8), then run flood-irrigation base and modern-irrigation district scenarios (Table 3, Fig. 10).
rows.notes: The study does report its own model runs, but the claimed effect (lower recharge under drip/modern irrigation than under flood irrigation) is not a finding: in Section 3.2 the authors simply set the recharge term to zero in any district assumed to switch to modern irrigation, on the grounds that modern irrigation is highly water-efficient, and reduce well pumping by 40% citing another study [16]. The model output (groundwater table decline of 10<U+2013>50 cm, largest in Tokh where the clay cap is shallow) follows directly from this input assumption; the scenario outputs are never compared with observations under drip or any modern irrigation. Only the flood-irrigation base case is calibrated to measured heads. The study also treats 'modern irrigation' generically (drip, sprinkler, subsurface) rather than drip specifically, though drip is named as one of the modern methods. Because the recharge reduction is assumed rather than measured or modelled, and the scenario result is unchecked against the real system, Q2 is answered no; a more lenient reader might count the calibrated-model scenario as model evidence. The study does state a conditioning factor (clay cap depth governs the magnitude of the decline; Conclusions) and a limitation (future domestic/industrial demands not considered; Discussion), but these are not scored given Q2 = no.

notes: Full text appears complete. Single-governorate MODFLOW/GMS study in the Nile Delta; recharge under modern irrigation is an imposed scenario value (zero), not an estimated or measured quantity; no dispersion measures reported for the head-decline results (only a range across districts in Fig. 10).
